title: A truckload of bananas can set off a port’s nuclear-smuggling alarm
body: Bananas are rich in potassium, and about 0.0117% of all potassium is the radioactive isotope potassium-40. A typical banana gives off roughly 15 decays per second, so a lorry full of them can trigger the radiation portal monitors that scan for smuggled nuclear material at US ports. Eating one is harmless: the dose is about **0.1 microsieverts**, and because your body keeps its potassium level steady, the extra is flushed out within hours rather than piling up. You are far more radioactive than a banana anyway: the potassium in an adult body manages around 5,400 decays every second.

slides.label: the ‘banana equivalent dose’ from eating one banana
slides.text: An informal unit invented to explain tiny doses. A chest CT scan is about 70,000 bananas; a lethal dose about 35 million.

slides.label: radioactive decays per second from the potassium in a 70 kg adult
slides.text: A banana manages about 15. By that measure you are worth roughly 360 bananas, every second of your life.

slides.heading: Other radioactive snacks
slides.text: Potatoes, kidney beans, sunflower seeds and nuts are rich in potassium-40 too. Brazil nuts go further: they can also contain radium, measured at up to 444 becquerels per kilogram. None of this is a health concern; it is a reminder that natural radioactivity is everywhere, including in us.

slides.question: Why doesn’t eating lots of bananas make you more radioactive over time?
slides.explanation: Your kidneys hold the body’s potassium level constant, so the extra potassium-40 from a banana is excreted within hours and the dose never accumulates.
